title: Influence: The Psychology of Persuasion
author: Robert B. Cialdini
blurb: Why do we agree to things we never meant to agree to? Social psychologist Robert Cialdini went undercover in sales teams, fundraising groups and advertising firms to find out. He found that most persuasion runs on a small set of automatic mental shortcuts. These shortcuts usually serve us well, because they let us decide quickly in a complicated world. But compliance professionals have learned to trigger them on purpose. Cialdini names six: reciprocation, commitment and consistency, social proof, liking, authority, and scarcity. For each one, he explains why it works, shows how it gets exploited, and offers a practical defense. The book is not anti-persuasion. Its message is that once you can spot these triggers, you can welcome honest influence and say no to manipulation.

lessons.b: Like animals responding to a single trigger feature, people often comply automatically when a familiar cue appears, and persuaders can exploit these mental shortcuts.

lessons.t: Reciprocation: The Pull of a Gift
lessons.b: We feel strongly obliged to repay what others give us, even uninvited gifts and concessions, so a small favor or a retreat to a smaller request can win an outsized yes.
